title: Why You Hear Your Name In A Noisy Room
sources: Moray 1959, Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology 11:56-60 (about a third heard own name in the ignored ear)
Wood & Cowan 1995, J. Exp. Psychology: Learning, Memory & Cognition 21:255-260 (replication, ~35 percent)
Conway, Cowan & Bunting 2001, Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 8:331-335 (65 percent low vs 20 percent high working memory capacity)

lines.text: You're deep in a loud party, and somewhere behind you, someone says your name.
You weren't even listening to them. So how did you hear it?
It's called the cocktail party effect.
Your brain secretly scans the noise you ignore, hunting for words that matter to you, like your name.
When scientists tested it in nineteen fifty-nine, only about one in three people noticed their name.
Later studies found people with weaker focus noticed it way more: sixty-five percent!
So hearing your name means your brain let a little extra sound slip in.
Next time someone calls your name, you'll know why!
